paras: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang reportedly spent decades publicly humiliating employees, making violent threats, and ridiculing people in front of their colleagues, sometimes calling the treatment a necessary part of working at the company.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s management style included publicly berating employees, making violent threats, and humiliating people in front of their colleagues, according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former employees conducted by New York Times, along with hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years.

The behavior reportedly dates back at least to 2004, when Michael Winston joined Nvidia as senior vice president of human resources. Within weeks, he witnessed Huang verbally attacking employees during a two-day company retreat attended by about 50 people. Winston later confronted Huang, warning that the conduct could expose Nvidia to lawsuits. Huang reportedly defended the public humiliation as a “rite of passage,” saying he subjected new employees to it during their first six months to see whether they could tolerate it.

paras: Representatives from nearly 200 countries are struggling to find agreement over fossil fuels and climate finance as talks stretched into a second day of overtime.
A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts in Antalya hoped would bridge the divide between nations.

pg:https://openthemagazine.com/world/exp.desc: In Antalya, negotiators have put a figure on how much warming to expect and how much carbon they hope to capture. The number they dropped was the $120 billion that developing countries wanted to help them live with the consequences
paras: By two o’clock on Sunday morning, the $120 billion target had gone. In its place was a proposal for a technical report. Governments would consider their options for a starting figure in November 2027. Elsewhere in those same ten pages, the authors had managed to be quite precise about money. Paragraph 19 put developing countries’ adaptation needs at $305 billion a year. The difficulty in Antalya was agreeing how much help those countries could count on.

The talks in Turkey were already into their second day of overtime. Murat Kurum, the Turkish environment minister presiding over COP31, believed he had a text governments could accept. Negotiators had about three hours to raise objections or suggest changes before the planned plenary, the Associated Press reported. European and Pacific delegations had been pressing to restore an explicit commitment to move away from fossil fuels. African negotiators wanted a figure they could take home. The presidency needed both groups, and the countries resisting their demands, to let the same document through.

Ghana’s environment minister, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, who chairs the African Group of negotiators, had already explained the mood on her side of the table. “We did not come here to beg,” she said, according to the BBC. Her objection went to the purpose of the money. Governments whose people had contributed relatively little to the warming were having to find room in their budgets for its consequences. They had come to Antalya to settle how much of that bill wealthy countries would share.

paras: Theresa May has said she feels “aghast” at Andy Burnham’s plan for potentially rejoining the EU, arguing in a rare interview that the prime minister should “accept Brexit and move on”.

paras: The 13-years-in-the-making Grand Theft Auto VI has been hailed for its of-the-moment touches, but it does have one quaintly anachronistic aspect: Nobody reaches for the aux. The game’s in-universe radio stations provide the soundtrack to its criminal and romantic endeavors, with drivers eschewing streaming and flipping the dial until they find their favorites. The United Nations climate summit in Turkey became the longest-ever UN climate conference on Sunday as negotiations over a final agreement descended into deadlock, with the European Union and several other countries formally rejecting the proposed text.

Pugh, who is a United Nations Patron of the Oceans, spent three days this week swimming parts of the dangerous waterway to highlight how the war with Iran threatens the area's habitat and wildlife.

On Sunday, nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas.

pg:https://www.ksat.com/news/world/2026/.desc: Going into this year’s U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low.
paras: NEW YORK – Going into this year’s U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. But the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected — a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures.

Gaining traction at this year’s summit, known as COP31, was always going to be difficult. Leaders and everyday people alike have plenty to contend with in addition to extreme weather, from wars to shaky economies to fears about artificial intelligence. Last year’s climate conference in Brazil, which had all the ingredients for an historic outcome, turned out to be a flop. And for the second year in a row, the United States, the world’s richest country and historically No. 1 polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the U.S. from climate negotiations.

Still, there was hope, among lifetime environmental campaigners, climate scientists and negotiators from many countries, that there would be some progress on confronting the main cause of climate change: coal, oil and gas.

paras: The United States Army is slated to conduct two controlled detonations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in the Midwestern state of Iowa, aiming to destroy 68 drums of degraded lead azide — a highly volatile, lead-based explosive used to trigger the main charges in some conventional munitions.
Announced just five days before an original Friday, November 20, detonation date, the Army’s decision was authorised by an emergency permit issued by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

Residents, environmental health experts, and Iowa elected officials have decried the detonation of lead-rich explosive material, citing scant public notice and potential environmental and health harms.

pg:https://www.streakingthelawn.com/foot.desc: ﻿Analyzing Virginia’s rout of the Tar Heels, which clinched back-to-back bowl trips for the first time since 2019.
paras: There is no getting around the fact that this year has been a disappointing one for Virginia football. That said, the ’Hoos entered Saturday one win from bowl eligibility. The 36-7 win over Cal snapped a three-game losing streak and got the Cavaliers to 5-5. North Carolina arrived at Scott Stadium in the exact same spot. Five ACC teams were sitting at 5-5 and one win from a bowl: Florida State, North Carolina, Stanford, Syracuse and Virginia. This game saw two of them facing off for the 131st time in the South’s Oldest Rivalry.

Bill Belichick’s Tar Heels came in shorthanded. Starting quarterback Billy Edwards Jr. was out with an undisclosed injury, so true freshman Travis Burgess, a four-star recruit who missed his senior season of high school with a torn ACL, made his first career start. Safety Greg Smith III, UNC’s leader in interceptions, sat out the first half after the ACC suspended him for his role in the brawl at the end of Carolina’s 16-14 loss to Louisville. Despite the absences, bettors were clearly on UNC in this game, as the DraftKings line moved from Virginia opening as a 1.5-point favorite to closing as a 1.5-point underdog.

However, from the jump it was clear Virginia had bad intentions and was determined not to let UNC hang around. Beau Pribula threw four touchdown passes, the ’Hoos led 20-10 at halftime and pulled away in the fourth quarter for a 41-24 win. Virginia moves to 6-5 (4-4 ACC). North Carolina falls to 5-6 (2-5) and has to beat NC State next week to go bowling.

pg:https://www.topgear.com/car-news/supe.desc: And it's not a limited-production rarity either. Welcome to the coolest 296 yet
paras: The 296 Challenge Stradale is combustion only. Ferrari has stripped out the electric motors and battery, reducing weight by 140kg and power by nearly 200bhp.

There’s a lot going on here. Traditionally Ferrari only builds one special version of its mid-engined cars. But this is the second derivative of the standard 296 GTB. Last year we had the 868bhp Speciale, now we have the 670bhp Challenge Stradale.

pg:https://greekreporter.com/2026/11/22/.desc: UN climate talks negotiations at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey collapsed without an agreement, exposing deep divisions between major economies
paras: The summit, jointly led by Turkey and Australia, ended after more than two weeks of negotiations, including an unprecedented extension of discussions beyond the scheduled closing date. The immediate breaking point was a final draft agreement that made no explicit reference to fossil fuels, the principal driver of climate change.

According to Reuters, the European Union and several other countries rejected the proposed text, arguing that it was too weak to deliver meaningful progress. COP31 President Murat Kurum acknowledged the failure, saying: “There is nothing to do, we did all that we could.” He subsequently confirmed that no further draft would be presented.

Ireland’s climate and energy minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the European Union, strongly criticized the proposal. As reported by Euronews, he declared: “We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya Pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels.”

The failure to agree on a common political text exposed widening divisions over how countries should respond to the climate crisis, even as several decisions under individual negotiating tracks were adopted.

paras: NEW YORK – Going into this year’s U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. But the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected — a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures.

Gaining traction at this year’s summit, known as COP31, was always going to be difficult. Leaders and everyday people alike have plenty to contend with in addition to extreme weather, from wars to shaky economies to fears about artificial intelligence. Last year’s climate conference in Brazil, which had all the ingredients for an historic outcome, turned out to be a flop. And for the second year in a row, the United States, the world’s richest country and historically No. 1 polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the U.S. from climate negotiations.

Still, there was hope, among lifetime environmental campaigners, climate scientists and negotiators from many countries, that there would be some progress on confronting the main cause of climate change: coal, oil and gas.

paras: The United Nations COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, has ended without an overarching political agreement after countries failed to reach consensus on fossil fuels, climate finance and the pace of global decarbonisation. Negotiations concluded on Sunday 22 November 2026, nearly two days after the scheduled finish, making COP31 the longest-running UN climate conference on record.

The European Union, UK and several other countries rejected the proposed final agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, arguing that it failed to confront the fossil fuels driving climate change. However, the summit was not without progress. Governments adopted separate decisions covering climate adaptation and a just transition, while businesses, investors and cities announced or highlighted new clean energy initiatives.

The contrasting outcomes raise an important question for responsible businesses. How can organisations deliver credible climate commitments and measurable environmental progress when international political consensus remains so difficult to achieve?

paras: The UN COP31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya ended on Sunday without a major political agreement, after deep divisions between countries over fossil fuels and finance for the poorest. It is the first time since the 2009 Copenhagen summit that the main declaration of one of these conferences has collapsed in this way.

Negotiations, due to end on Friday, ran into Sunday, making COP31 the longest UN climate conference in history, according to the BBC. The final draft, presented in the early hours, did not mention “fossil fuels”, the main cause of global warming, and referred only indirectly to the commitment made at COP28 in 2023 to “transition away” from them in energy systems. An earlier draft mentioned them six times, which was unacceptable to oil-producing countries.

The European Union, Pacific island states and others rejected the text. “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels,” said the EU's representative, Irish minister Darragh O'Brien. Panama and the Marshall Islands also criticised its lack of ambition. At the other end, Saudi Arabia's delegate, Mohammad Ayoub, said Arab countries had negotiated “in good faith” and noted that they account for only a small share of historical emissions, while Russia warned that moving away from fossil fuels too quickly would cause “fuel poverty”.

paras: On the evening of November 20, in Türkiye’s Mediterranean beach city of Antalya, journalists began packing their laptops, dismantling television equipment, and preparing to leave the venue of the United Nations climate summit. Behind closed doors, negotiators from nearly 200 countries were still arguing over the wording of the summit’s final political text.

The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) was scheduled to end that Friday. The media centre, which had accommodated thousands of journalists during the fortnight, was gradually emptying. Camera crews prepared their final transmissions, and delegates checked flights and hotel bookings. There was still no final declaration to report.

Outside, Antalya went about its day. Trams ran through the city, and tourists walked the cobbled streets of the historic Kaleiçi quarter, with the old harbour beyond. Inside, diplomats were struggling to agree on a response to a crisis that threatens coastlines, livelihoods, and entire nations.

Good morning. The world’s nations have failed to reach agreement at the Cop31 talks in Turkey. In a dramatic conclusion to the summit, major powers rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels. The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien.

What was in the proposed agreement? The Antalya pact invited nations to electrify their economies, called on wealthy countries to fund climate adaptation for poorer ones, and urged signatories to minimise any “overshoot” of the Paris agreement’s 1.5C global heating threshold. However, it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” demanded by more than 130 countries, instead including controversial provisions on carbon capture and storage technology that critics argued would perpetuate fossil fuel use.

paras: It was a day-and-a-half past the official deadline when the UN climate summit COP31 began to unravel in earnest.

On Sunday morning, the corridors inside the huge expo-style venue in the Turkish city of Antalya were almost empty. Tired groups of delegates and media sat propped against the walls waiting for updates, charging their phones and drinking coffee. Many had barely slept. Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen – who headed up the COP31 negotiations – reportedly slept for only a few minutes on the final night, as delegates kept waking him.
The talks dragged well into overtime to become the longest summit on record. But it would not finish the way co-presidents Bowen and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum had hoped.

pg:https://theconversation.com/cop31-why.desc: Negotiations broke down over whether to directly address fossil fuels, leaving the most climate-vulnerable nations deeply disappointed.
paras: The UN’s annual two-week climate summit, Cop31, has ended in failure. Countries could not find consensus on a final agreement. It is the first such failure in more than 20 years.

The summit started relatively smoothly. In fact, the conference agenda was adopted within a few hours on day one, as country parties found nothing objectionable. At the time, this event looked like it might be smooth sailing: another summit simply focused on implementing policies agreed in previous years.

But week two became explosive. First, the draft agreement – which if adopted would have been known as the Antalya Accords – conceded that we have failed to keep global temperature rise below 1.5˚C and that the world is entering a period of “overshoot”. Second, oil and gas producing nations fought to keep the root cause of climate change – namely fossil fuels – out of any deal. And they succeeded, as the agreement fell through.

pg:https://theconversation.com/how-did-t.desc: Division over fossil fuels at this year’s UN climate summit scotched any hope of a deal – despite Australian efforts.
paras: Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Turkey, have come to an end – but not as we might have hoped.

Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt, shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners.

In a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming, the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment.

pg:https://www.courthousenews.com/un-cli.desc: It hasn't happened since 2009: International talks to fight climate change ended without any new pledges and commitments.
paras: It hasn't happened since 2009: International talks to fight climate change ended without any new pledges and commitments.

The summit, held this year in Antalya, Turkey, and known as COP31, was overshadowed by geopolitical tensions and wars, the withdrawal of U.S. President Donald Trump from the United Nations process to tackle climate change and growing alarm over the accelerating pace of global warming.

On Sunday, with the faltering talks already in overtime, the EU delegation walked out of the negotiations and said it could not accept a final declaration that did include language over the need to transition away from fossil fuels. The United Kingdom and many developing nations also rejected the proposed text as unacceptable.

paras: The True Crime Community, known as the TCC by its members, is a growing online community of young people who idolize and romanticize mass shooters.

Allizandra Herberhold is a licensed social worker who's spent two years undercover on social media platforms studying the TCC and its members. Herberhold is what's called a "deradicalizer" and has helped 18 kids leave the TCC. She says most kids age out of the dark interest in violence, but some need extra help.

Herberhold said most kids inside the TCC are desperate for community, outsiders who are often bullied at school, isolated, and dealing with trouble at home. And like the past mass shooters they idolize, many are battling mental health issues and have a history of self harm.

pg:https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/11/23/c.desc: Leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process.
paras: Leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process. The conference ended without consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact—the overarching political agreement for the COP31 climate summit.

I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story. “Walande… the birthplace written in my passport, no longer exists,” he told a hushed room. “It is submerged beneath the waves.” His words moved the high-level event’s moderator to tears.

COP31’s inability to reach an overarching agreement leaves communities like Walande—and hundreds of other communities that have been forced to relocate—to face consequences of the climate crisis on their own. Despite coordinated calls from civil society, related outcome decisions do not include explicit discussion of displacement and planned relocation, and governments failed to increase funding to help frontline communities adapt. Nor was there recognition of the International Court of Justice’s landmark opinion affirming that governments have human rights obligations to address the climate crisis.

pg:https://time.com/article/2026/11/23/c.desc: Don't confuse the lack of another global accord with the lack of international engagement to tackle climate change.
paras: Participants sleep under COP31 signage in the main hall on the final day of the COP31 UNFCCC Climate Conference on Nov. 20 in Antalya, Turkey.

In the eleven years since the Paris Agreement, countries around the world have met annually to plot out the global consensus on how to tackle climate change. In some years negotiations led to big breakthroughs. In others, talks simply kept the ball in play, signaling to the world that nations were aligned in their desire to tackle climate change, even if it’s hard to agree on the exact path forward.

So it was a striking moment in the three-decade arc of United Nations climate negotiations when talks fell apart in Turkey over the weekend at this year’s COP31. The decade-long global consensus about the urgency of tackling climate change that produced the Paris Agreement at COP21 in 2015, it seems, came to an end on Sunday. The issues at play were many, of various levels of complexity, but the biggest was rather simple: a group of countries led by Saudi Arabia and Russia resisted reference to phasing out fossil fuels in the final text, and a bloc of 130 countries including the European Union refused to sign on without it.

pg:https://www.dailybreeze.com/2026/11/2.desc: It’s become all but impossible to have the words “fossil fuels” show up in a final agreement.
paras: NEW YORK (AP) — Going into this year’s U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. But the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected — a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures.

Gaining traction at this year’s summit, known as COP31, was always going to be difficult. Leaders and everyday people alike have plenty to contend with in addition to extreme weather, from wars to shaky economies to fears about artificial intelligence. Last year’s climate conference in Brazil, which had all the ingredients for a historic outcome, turned out to be a flop. And for the second year in a row, the United States, the world’s richest country and historically No. 1 polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the U.S. from climate negotiations.

Still, there was hope, among lifetime environmental campaigners, climate scientists and negotiators from many countries, that there would be some progress on confronting the main cause of climate change: coal, oil and gas.
There are few ways to dress it up: COP31 was a deeply disappointing outcome for the future of the planet – called by many the “worst COP ever”.

After two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, governments failed to agree the overarching political declaration (the cover decision), while progress on other issues was either negligible or the can kicked down the road.

Second, adaptation finance. Last year, countries committed to at least tripling finance for adaptation by 2035. COP31 failed to establish a credible plan for delivering this. There was no agreed baseline, no meaningful delivery timetable and no clarity about where the money would come from. For communities already experiencing increasingly devastating floods, droughts and extreme heat, another year of delay is not an abstract diplomatic failure. It has real consequences for people’s lives and livelihoods.

pg:https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/20.desc: The failure exposes a diplomacy that protects fossil-fuel power while leaving vulnerable countries to pay the price.
paras: COP31 ended without an overarching agreement on Sunday in Antalya, Turkiye, after nearly 200 countries failed to agree on a final climate pact. The proposed text could not even name the principal cause of global warming: fossil fuels. The European Union, several Pacific island states and other governments rejected it, while oil-producing countries resisted stronger language. After three decades of annual summits, this was the first such breakdown since 2009.

It is tempting to call this an extraordinary diplomatic failure. But the collapse reveals something more enduring. Climate negotiations have become remarkably effective at keeping governments at the table while avoiding the economic changes that meaningful climate action requires. The system is not designed literally to produce no agreements; it is designed to accommodate interests powerful enough to prevent decisive ones.

Consider what happened in Antalya. The EU objected that the final draft did not even mention fossil fuels. Yet the omission was not a clerical oversight. Earlier language on moving away from oil, gas and coal had been weakened as negotiations proceeded. The summit could not agree on how to implement the agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. What should have been the starting point for action became the point at which diplomacy broke down.

pg:https://legal-planet.org/2026/11/23/w.desc: The Drain is a roundup of environmental and climate news from Legal Planet. This week we report from COP31.
paras: This year’s edition of the annual United Nations climate talks known as COP31 — the thirty-first Conference of the Parties — ended in spectacular failure on Sunday. There was no final agreement on the way forward in the fight against climate change, and a growing global divide was on full display — the divide between nations that are interested in charting a path away from fossil fuels and those governments that want to continue full-speed-ahead toward a dramatically warmer world thanks to prolonged dependence on their production of oil, gas, and coal.

Remember that just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai all countries did agree to “transition away from fossil fuels in a just, orderly and equitable manner,” as outgoing UN Secretary General António Guterres noted, expressing disappointment with this week’s outcome.
Sadly, a conference with the motto “Where dialogue becomes action” emblazoned on billboards all over the city ended in none — at least when it comes to the formal negotiations.
